e-12567.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+t^2\,\mathbf j+t^3\,\mathbf k$ at the point $P(1,1,1).$
e-12567.worked_solution:
The point $P(1,1,1)$ is at the tip of $\mathbf r(t)$ for some specific value $t_0$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector $\mathbf r'(t_0)$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\,i+\,j+\,k \\ t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+{t}^{3}\,k & =i+\,j+\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $\mathbf i, \mathbf j,$ and $\mathbf k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}t=1 \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ {t}^{3}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,1,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r(1).$  

Now, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,k \\  & =i+2t\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =i+2(1)\,j+3(1)^{2}\,k \\  & =i+2\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at at the point $P(1,1,1)$ is $\,\mathbf i+2\,\mathbf j+3\,\mathbf k.$

e-12568.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
e-12568.problem: Find a parametrization of the tangent line to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t},\: 4t^2\right\rangle$ at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
e-12568.worked_solution:
Let  $P$ be the point at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ).$  At this point,  the vector $\mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf R(u)=\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )+u \, \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

 

First, we find $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,4{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}⟩=⟨0,1,{\pi }^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now,  we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,8t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,8(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,4\pi ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P$ where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(u)=⟨0,1,{\pi }^{2}⟩+u⟨-1,0,4\pi ⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14078039/assets/e24b811fb8d9e43bd0682e3686f8b2ef1198e36016978ca305a7df4dffe21889.png)

e-12580.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
e-12580.problem: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^2+1\,,\, 6t+3\right\rangle,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle.$
e-12580.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,6⟩ & =0 \\ 3\cdot 2t+1\cdot 6 & =0 \\ 6t+6 & =0 \\ t & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{2}+1\,,\,6(-1)+3⟩=⟨2\,,\,-3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(2,-3).$

e-12569.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
e-12569.problem: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=(t^2+t)\,\mathbf i+(t^2-t)\,\mathbf j,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j.$
e-12569.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,j \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $\mathbf r'(t)=c(3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j=c(3\,i+\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2t+1=3c \\ 2t-1=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $c=2t-1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2t+1 & =3c \\ 2t+1 & =3(2t-1) \\ 2t+1 & =6t-3 \\ 6t-2t & =1+3 \\ 4t & =4 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf r'$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =({1}^{2}+1)\,i+({1}^{2}-1)\,j=2\,i,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel at the point $(2,0).$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}-1,{t}^{2}+1⟩$ at the point where $t=-2.$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=-2,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(-2)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(-2) & =⟨3(-2)^{2},2(-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨12,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=-2$ is $⟨12,-4⟩.$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=2\sqrt{3-t}\,i+(1-2t)\,j+(t+3)\,k$ at the point $P(2,-3,5).$
after.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,-3,5)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\ 2\sqrt{3-t}\,i+(1-2t)\,j+(t+3)\,k & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3-t}=2 \\ 1-2t=-3 \\ t+3=5\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $t=2.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,-3,5)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(2).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{3-t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+3)\,k \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-t}}\,i-2\,j+k \\ {r}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-2}}\,i-2\,j+k \\  & =-\,i-2\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,-3,5)$ is $-\,i-2\,j+k.$

content.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=2\sqrt{3-t}\,i+(1-2t)\,j+(t+3)\,k$ at the point $P(2,-3,5).$
content.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,-3,5)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\ 2\sqrt{3-t}\,i+(1-2t)\,j+(t+3)\,k & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3-t}=2 \\ 1-2t=-3 \\ t+3=5\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $t=2.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,-3,5)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(2).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{3-t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+3)\,k \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-t}}\,i-2\,j+k \\ {r}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-2}}\,i-2\,j+k \\  & =-\,i-2\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,-3,5)$ is $-\,i-2\,j+k.$

after.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+j+k \\ (3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k & =2\,i+j+k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3t+2=2 \\ 6t+1=1 \\ 1-4{t}^{2}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j-8t\,k \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =3\,i+6\,j-8(0)\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,1,1)$ is $3\,i+6\,j.$

content.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=(3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k$ at the point $P(2,1,1).$
content.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+j+k \\ (3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k & =2\,i+j+k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3t+2=2 \\ 6t+1=1 \\ 1-4{t}^{2}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j-8t\,k \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =3\,i+6\,j-8(0)\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,1,1)$ is $3\,i+6\,j.$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t},\,{t}^{2}⟩$ at the point where $t=0.$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{-t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-{e}^{-t},\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,-{e}^{-0},\,2\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is $⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩.$

Question 4
?

Find a tangent vector to the curve r(t)=⟨et,e−t,t2⟩ at the point where t=0.

a
⟨0,1,−1⟩
b
⟨1,1,0⟩
c
⟨0,−1,−1⟩
d
⟨1,0,−1⟩
e
⟨1,−1,0⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=0, the vector r′(0) is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate r′(t) and evaluate it at t=0: r′(t)=⟨ddtet,ddte−t,ddtt2⟩=⟨et,−e−t,2t⟩r′(0)=⟨e0,−e−0,2⋅0⟩=⟨1,−1,0⟩ Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where t=0 is ⟨1,−1,0⟩.

verification.explanation: Differentiating gives r'(t)=⟨e^t,-e^(-t),2t⟩, so r'(0)=⟨1,-1,0⟩. The revealed solution confirms option e. The deliberately submitted option d is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Vector
content.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t},\,{t}^{2}⟩$ at the point where $t=0.$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{-t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-{e}^{-t},\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,-{e}^{-0},\,2\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is $⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩.$

Question 5
?

Find a vector that's tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨2(t−sin⁡t),2(t−cos⁡t)⟩ at the point where t=π.

a
⟨−2,2⟩
b
⟨4,−2⟩
c
⟨4,4⟩
d
⟨2,2⟩
e
⟨4,2⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Differentiate: r'(t)=⟨2(1-cos(t)),2(1+sin(t))⟩. Since cos(π)=-1 and sin(π)=0, r'(π)=⟨4,2⟩. Thus option e is a tangent vector.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨2(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,2(t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi .$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi $,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[2(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)],\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[2(t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)]⟩ \\  & =⟨2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,2(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ),\,2(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨2(1-(-1)),\,2(1+0)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $  is  $⟨4,\,2⟩$

Find a vector that's tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨2(t−sin⁡t),2(t−cos⁡t)⟩ at the point where t=π.

a
⟨−2,2⟩
b
⟨4,−2⟩
c
⟨4,4⟩
d
⟨2,2⟩
e
⟨4,2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=π, the vector r′(π) is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate r′(t) and evaluate it at t=π: r′(t)=⟨ddt[2(t−sin⁡t)],ddt[2(t−cos⁡t)]⟩=⟨2(1−cos⁡t),2(1+sin⁡t)⟩r′(π)=⟨2(1−cos⁡π),2(1+sin⁡π)⟩=⟨2(1−(−1)),2(1+0)⟩=⟨4,2⟩

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where t=π is ⟨4,2⟩

At the point where $t=\pi $,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[2(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)],\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[2(t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)]⟩ \\  & =⟨2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,2(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ),\,2(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨2(1-(-1)),\,2(1+0)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $  is  $⟨4,\,2⟩$

 ⟨0,1⟩+u⟨2,0⟩

c
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨2,−5⟩

⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,−5⟩
e
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,−5⟩

decision.explanation: At t=0, r(0)=⟨0,1⟩. Differentiating gives r'(t)=⟨2t/(t²+1),-5⟩, hence r'(0)=⟨0,-5⟩. The tangent line is r(0)+u r'(0)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,-5⟩ for all real u.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1),1-5t⟩$ at the point where $t=0,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+1),1-5(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-5t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1},-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+1},-5⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,-5⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨ln⁡(t2+1),1−5t⟩ at the point where t=0, valid for all real values of u?

a
 ⟨0,1⟩+u⟨2,0⟩
b
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨2,0⟩
c
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨2,−5⟩
d
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,−5⟩
e
⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,−5⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=0, the vector r′(0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(0)+ur′(0),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(0): r(0)=⟨ln⁡(02+1),1−5(0)⟩=⟨0,1⟩

Now, we calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(ln⁡(t2+1)),ddt(1−5t)⟩=⟨2tt2+1,−5⟩

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=0: r′(0)=⟨2(0)02+1,−5⟩=⟨0,−5⟩

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=0 is
R(u)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,−5⟩,u∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: We have r(0)=⟨0,1⟩ and r'(0)=⟨0,-5⟩. Thus the tangent line is r(0)+u r'(0)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,-5⟩ for every real u, confirming option e and the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1),1-5t⟩$ at the point where $t=0,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+1),1-5(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-5t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1},-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+1},-5⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,-5⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=ti+(t3+1)j+t5k at the point P(1,2,1), valid for real values of u?

a
i+2j+k+u(i+3j+4k)
b
i+2j+k+u(i+j+4k)
c
i+j+k+u(i+3j+5k)
d
i+2j+k+u(i+4j+5k)
e
i+2j+k+u(i+3j+5k)
Submit

decision.explanation: The point P(1,2,1) corresponds to t=1. Differentiating gives r'(t)=i+3t²j+5t⁴k, so r'(1)=i+3j+5k. The tangent line is r(1)+u r'(1), which is option e.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j+{t}^{5}\,k$ at the point $P(1,2,1),$ 
valid for real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
The point $P(1,2,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+2\,j+k \\ t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j+{t}^{5}\,k & =i+2\,j+k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}t=1 \\ {t}^{3}+1=2 \\ {t}^{5}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,2,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{5})\,k \\  & =i+3{t}^{2}\,j+5{t}^{4}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1) & =i+3(1)^{2}\,j+5(1)^{4}\,k \\  & =i+3\,j+5\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(1,2,1)$ is 

$$
R(u)=i+2\,j+\,k+u(\,i+3\,j+5\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=ti+(t3+1)j+t5k at the point P(1,2,1), valid for real values of u?

a
i+2j+k+u(i+3j+4k)
b
i+2j+k+u(i+j+4k)
c
i+j+k+u(i+3j+5k)
d
i+2j+k+u(i+4j+5k)
e
i+2j+k+u(i+3j+5k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The point P(1,2,1) is at the tip of r(t) for some specific value t0 of the parameter t. At this point, the vector r′(t0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(t0)+ur′(t0),u∈(−∞,∞).

First, we find the value of t that corresponds to P. We know that

r(t)=i+2j+kti+(t3+1)j+t5k=i+2j+k,

and equating the coefficients of i,j, and k yields the following system:

{t=1t3+1=2t5=1

From the first equation, we get t=1. This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, P(1,2,1) is at the tip of the vector r(1).

We calculate r′(t):

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(t3+1)j+ddt(t5)k=i+3t2j+5t4k

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=1:

r′(1)=i+3(1)2j+5(1)4k=i+3j+5k

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point P(1,2,1) is R(u)=i+2j+k+u(i+3j+5k),u∈(−∞,∞).

content.problem:
Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j+{t}^{5}\,k$ at the point $P(1,2,1),$ 
valid for real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
The point $P(1,2,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+2\,j+k \\ t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j+{t}^{5}\,k & =i+2\,j+k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}t=1 \\ {t}^{3}+1=2 \\ {t}^{5}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,2,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{5})\,k \\  & =i+3{t}^{2}\,j+5{t}^{4}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1) & =i+3(1)^{2}\,j+5(1)^{4}\,k \\  & =i+3\,j+5\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(1,2,1)$ is 

$$
R(u)=i+2\,j+\,k+u(\,i+3\,j+5\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

before.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩ at the point where t=π, valid for all real values of u?

a
⟨1,1⟩+u⟨−1,0⟩
b
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩
c
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨−1,1⟩
d
⟨1,1⟩+u⟨0,1⟩
e
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨−1,0⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: At t=π, r(π)=⟨-1,0⟩. Differentiating gives r'(t)=⟨-sin(t),-cos(t)⟩, so r'(π)=⟨0,1⟩. Thus the tangent line is ⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩ for all real u.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩ at the point where t=π, valid for all real values of u?

a
⟨1,1⟩+u⟨−1,0⟩
b
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩
c
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨−1,1⟩
d
⟨1,1⟩+u⟨0,1⟩
e
⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨−1,0⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=π, the vector r′(π) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(π)+ur′(π),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(π): r(π)=⟨cos⁡π,−sin⁡π⟩=⟨−1,0⟩

Now, we calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(cos⁡t),ddt(−sin⁡t)⟩=⟨−sin⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=π: r′(π)=⟨−sin⁡π,−cos⁡π⟩=⟨0,1⟩

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=π is
R(u)=⟨−1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,u∈(−∞,∞).

verification.explanation: r(π)=⟨-1,0⟩ and r'(π)=⟨-sin(π),-cos(π)⟩=⟨0,1⟩. Therefore the tangent line is ⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩ for all real u, confirming option b and the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Question 9

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=⟨3t+5,1−t3⟩ at the point where t=0, valid for all real values of u?

a
⟨3,−1⟩+u⟨1,5⟩
b
⟨5,1⟩+u⟨3,−3⟩
c
⟨3,−1⟩+u⟨3,0⟩
d
⟨5,1⟩+u⟨3,0⟩
e
⟨5,1⟩+u⟨1,5⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At the point where t=0, the vector r′(0) is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at P can be parametrized as R(u)=r(0)+ur′(0),u∈(−∞,∞)

First, we find r(0): r(0)=⟨3(0)+5,1−03⟩=⟨5,1⟩

Now, we calculate r′(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(3t+5),ddt(1−t3)⟩=⟨3,−3t2⟩

Then, we evaluate r′(t) at t=0: r′(0)=⟨3,−3(0)2⟩=⟨3,0⟩

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where t=0 is
R(u)=⟨5,1⟩+u⟨3,0⟩,u∈(−∞,∞).

before.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj+sin2tk at the point corresponding to t=π4, valid for all real values of u?

a
i+j+12k+u(2i−j+k)
b
i+j+12k+u(i−j+12k)
c
i+j+12k+u(i+2j+12k)
d
i+j+12k+u(i−j+k)
e
i+j+12k+u(−i+2j+k)
Submit

decision.explanation: At t=π/4, r(t)=i+j+(1/2)k. Differentiating gives r'(t)=√2 cos(t)i−√2 sin(t)j+2sin(t)cos(t)k, which equals i−j+k at π/4. Thus r(π/4)+u r'(π/4) is option d, valid for all real u.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{sin}^{2}t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
after.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

 

$$
R(u)=r(\frac{\pi }{4})+u{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j+{sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}t)\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j-\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})k \\  & =\,i-\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
R(u)=\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k+u(\,i-\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

?

Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve r(t)=2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj+sin2tk at the point corresponding to t=π4, valid for all real values of u?

a
i+j+12k+u(2i−j+k)

c

content.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{sin}^{2}t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
content.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

 

$$
R(u)=r(\frac{\pi }{4})+u{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j+{sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}t)\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j-\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})k \\  & =\,i-\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
R(u)=\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k+u(\,i-\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨2t,2⟩. Perpendicularity requires ⟨2t,2⟩·⟨1,-2⟩=2t-4=0, giving only t=2. Then r(2)=⟨5,3⟩, so the only point is (5,3).

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1\,,\,2t-1⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,2⟩ & =0 \\ 1\cdot 2t+(-2)\cdot 2 & =0 \\ 2t-4 & =0 \\ 2(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨{(2)}^{2}+1\,,\,2(2)-1⟩=⟨5\,,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(5,3).$

Question 11
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t2+1,2t−1⟩, find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector ⟨1,−2⟩.

a
 (2,−3)
b
 (2,−3) and (10,5)
c
 (1,−1)
d
(5,3)
e
 (1,−1) and (5,3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(t2+1),ddt(2t−1)⟩=⟨2t,2⟩

The vectors ⟨1,−2⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if ⟨1,−2⟩⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have

⟨1,−2⟩⋅r′(t)=0⟨1,−2⟩⋅⟨2t,2⟩=01⋅2t+(−2)⋅2=02t−4=02(t−2)=0.

Therefore, the only solution is t=2.

Finally, since

r(2)=⟨(2)2+1,2(2)−1⟩=⟨5,3⟩,

we conclude that ⟨1,−2⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (5,3).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1\,,\,2t-1⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,2⟩ & =0 \\ 1\cdot 2t+(-2)\cdot 2 & =0 \\ 2t-4 & =0 \\ 2(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨{(2)}^{2}+1\,,\,2(2)-1⟩=⟨5\,,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(5,3).$

Question 12
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t2+2t,4−t2⟩, find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector ⟨0,−1⟩.

a
(3,3)
b
(0,4)
c
(3,3) and (0,4)
d
(−1,3)
e
(1,−4) and (−1,3)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨2t+2,-2t⟩. Perpendicularity requires r'(t)·⟨0,-1⟩=2t=0, so t=0 is the only solution. Since r(0)=⟨0,4⟩ and r'(0)=⟨2,0⟩ is nonzero, the only point is (0,4).

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+2t,4-{t}^{2}⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨0,-1⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+2,-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨2t+2,-2t⟩ & =0 \\ 0(2t+2)+(-1)(-2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{2}+2(0),4-{0}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,4).$

Question 12
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t2+2t,4−t2⟩, find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector ⟨0,−1⟩.

a
(3,3)
b
(0,4)
c
(3,3) and (0,4)
d
(−1,3)
e
(1,−4) and (−1,3)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=⟨ddt(t2+2t),ddt(4−t2)⟩=⟨2t+2,−2t⟩

The vectors ⟨0,−1⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if ⟨0,−1⟩⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have ⟨0,−1⟩⋅r′(t)=0⟨0,−1⟩⋅⟨2t+2,−2t⟩=00(2t+2)+(−1)(−2t)=02t=0t=0.

Therefore, the only solution is t=0.

Finally, since r(0)=⟨02+2(0),4−02⟩=⟨0,4⟩, we conclude that ⟨0,−1⟩ and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (0,4).

verification.explanation: r'(t)=⟨2t+2,-2t⟩, so its dot product with ⟨0,-1⟩ is 2t. This vanishes only at t=0, where r(0)=⟨0,4⟩ and the tangent vector is nonzero. The revealed solution confirms option b.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+2t,4-{t}^{2}⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨0,-1⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+2,-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨2t+2,-2t⟩ & =0 \\ 0(2t+2)+(-1)(-2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{2}+2(0),4-{0}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,4).$

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t2−1,t3+1⟩,t∈(−∞,0) find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector ⟨2,1⟩.

a
 (43,169)
b
 (0,0) and (43,169)
c
 (0,0)
d
 (79,−3727)
e
 (3,−7) and (79,−3727)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨2t,3t²⟩. Perpendicularity requires r'(t)·⟨2,1⟩=4t+3t²=t(4+3t)=0. Since t<0, only t=-4/3 is allowed. Evaluating r(-4/3) gives (7/9,-37/27), so option d contains all qualifying points.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1\,,\,{t}^{3}+1⟩,t\in (-\infty ,0)$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨2\,,\,1⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨2\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ 2\cdot 2t+1\cdot 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t(4+3t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (-\infty ,0)$, the only solution is $t=-\frac{4}{3}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-\frac{4}{3}) & =⟨{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-1\,,\,{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{3}+1⟩=⟨\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨2\,,\,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}).$

The vectors  $⟨2\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ 2\cdot 2t+1\cdot 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t(4+3t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (-\infty ,0)$, the only solution is $t=-\frac{4}{3}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-\frac{4}{3}) & =⟨{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-1\,,\,{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{3}+1⟩=⟨\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨2\,,\,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}).$

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨1,t/√(t²+1)⟩. Thus r'(t)·r(t)=(t+2)+t=2t+2, which is zero only when t=-1. Evaluating r(-1) gives (1,√2), so option a is the complete answer.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j]\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j) & =0 \\ (t+2)\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}} & =0 \\ t+2+t & =0 \\ 2t+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=-1.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1)=(-1+2)\,i+\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+1}\,j=i+\sqrt{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,\sqrt{2}).$

EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t): r′(t)=ddt(t+2)i+ddt(t2+1)j=i+tt2+1j

The vectors r(t) and r′(t) are perpendicular for some value of the parameter t if and only if r(t)⋅r′(t)=0. So, we have

r(t)⋅r′(t)=0[(t+2)i+t2+1j]⋅(i+tt2+1j)=0(t+2)⋅1+t2+1⋅tt2+1=0t+2+t=02t+2=0.

Therefore, the only solution is t=−1.

Finally, since

r(−1)=(−1+2)i+(−1)2+1j=i+2j,

we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are perpendicular at the point (1,2).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j]\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j) & =0 \\ (t+2)\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}} & =0 \\ t+2+t & =0 \\ 2t+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=-1.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1)=(-1+2)\,i+\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+1}\,j=i+\sqrt{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,\sqrt{2}).$

Question 15

Given the curve r(t)=ti+(1+12t2)j, find all of the points at which r′(t) and r(t) are perpendicular.

a
(0,1) and (2,3)
b
(0,1), (2,2), and (−2,2)
c
(2,3) and (−2,3)
d
(2,3)
e
(0,1)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨1,t⟩, so r(t)·r'(t)=t+t(1+t²/2)=t(2+t²/2). The second factor is positive for every real t, so only t=0 satisfies perpendicularity. Thus the only point is r(0)=(0,1).

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j]\cdot (i+t\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\cdot t & =0 \\ 2t+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{3} & =0 \\ t(4+{t}^{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0$ since $4+{t}^{2}>0$ for any $t.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)=0\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})\,j=j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,1).$

content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j]\cdot (i+t\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\cdot t & =0 \\ 2t+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{3} & =0 \\ t(4+{t}^{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0$ since $4+{t}^{2}>0$ for any $t.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)=0\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})\,j=j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,1).$

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{4}+4t\,,\,{t}^{3}-2t\,,\,2{t}^{3}-3t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =⟨0\,,\,c\,,\,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4{t}^{3}+4=0 \\ 3{t}^{2}-2=c \\ 6{t}^{2}-3=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $t=-1.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=1.$
These values also satisfy the third equation. 

Therefore, $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{4}+4(-1)\,,\,(-1)^{3}-2(-1)\,,\,2(-1)^{3}-3(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,1,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-3,1,1).$

Question 16
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t4+4t,t3−2t,2t3−3t⟩, find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector ⟨0,1,3⟩.

a
(−3,1,1)
b
 (5,−1,−1) and (−3,1,1)
c
 (5,−1,−1)
d
 (0,0,0) and (−3,1,1)
e
 (24,4,10)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t):

r′(t)=⟨ddt(t4+4t),ddt(t3−2t),ddt(2t3−3t)⟩=⟨4t3+4,3t2−2,6t2−3⟩

The vectors r′(t) and ⟨0,1,3⟩ are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r′(t0)=c⟨0,1,3⟩. So, we have

r′(t)=c⟨0,1,3⟩⟨4t3+4,3t2−2,6t2−3⟩=c⟨0,1,3⟩⟨4t3+4,3t2−2,6t2−3⟩=⟨0,c,3c⟩.

Equating the components gives:

{4t3+4=03t2−2=c6t2−3=3c

From the first equation, we obtain that t=−1. Substituting to the second equation, we get c=1. These values also satisfy the third equation.

Therefore, ⟨0,1,3⟩ and r′ are parallel only at the point corresponding to t=−1.

Finally, since r(−1)=⟨(−1)4+4(−1),(−1)3−2(−1),2(−1)3−3(−1)⟩=⟨−3,1,1⟩,

we conclude that ⟨0,1,3⟩ and r′(t) are parallel at the point (−3,1,1).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{4}+4t\,,\,{t}^{3}-2t\,,\,2{t}^{3}-3t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =⟨0\,,\,c\,,\,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4{t}^{3}+4=0 \\ 3{t}^{2}-2=c \\ 6{t}^{2}-3=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $t=-1.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=1.$
These values also satisfy the third equation. 

Therefore, $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{4}+4(-1)\,,\,(-1)^{3}-2(-1)\,,\,2(-1)^{3}-3(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,1,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-3,1,1).$

Question 17
?

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t2−2t,t2,8t−2t2⟩, find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector ⟨1,2,0⟩.

a
 (−1,1,6)
b
 (0,0,0) and (0,4,8)
c
 (3,1,−10) and (−1,1,6)
d
 (3,1,−10)
e
(0,4,8)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨2t-2,2t,8-4t⟩. Parallelism to ⟨1,2,0⟩ requires 8-4t=0, so t=2. Then r'(2)=⟨2,4,0⟩=2⟨1,2,0⟩ and r(2)=⟨0,4,8⟩. Thus option e is correct.

after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t-2{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =⟨c\,,\,2c\,,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2t-2=c \\ 2t=2c \\ 8-4t=0\end{aligned}

From the third equation, we obtain that $t=2.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=2.$

Question 17

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t2−2t,t2,8t−2t2⟩, find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector ⟨1,2,0⟩.

a
 (−1,1,6)
b
 (0,0,0) and (0,4,8)
c
 (3,1,−10) and (−1,1,6)
d
 (3,1,−10)
e
(0,4,8)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t):

r′(t)=⟨ddt(t2−2t),ddt(t2),ddt(8t−2t2)⟩=⟨2t−2,2t,8−4t⟩

The vectors r′(t) and ⟨0,1,3⟩ are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r′(t0)=c⟨1,2,0⟩. So, we have

r′(t)=c⟨1,2,0⟩⟨2t−2,2t,8−4t⟩=c⟨1,2,0⟩⟨2t−2,2t,8−4t⟩=⟨c,2c,0⟩.

Equating the components gives:

{2t−2=c2t=2c8−4t=0

From the third equation, we obtain that t=2. Substituting to the second equation, we get c=2. These values also satisfy the first equation.

Therefore, ⟨1,2,0⟩ and r′ are parallel only at the point corresponding to t=2.

Finally, since r(2)=⟨22−2(2),22,8(2)−2(2)2⟩=⟨0,4,8⟩,

we conclude that ⟨1,2,0⟩ and r′(t) are parallel at the point (0,4,8).

Question 18

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t3,et,et−1⟩, find all points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
(1,0,e−1) and (27,e3,e2)
b
(27,e3,e2)
c
(0,1,0) and (27,e3,e2)
d
(0,1,e−1) and (27,e3,e2)
e
(0,1,e−1)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨3t²,e^t,e^(t-1)⟩. Since e^t is nonzero, r'(t)=c r(t) requires c=1. Thus 3t²=t³, or t²(t-3)=0, giving t=0 and t=3. Their points are (0,1,e^(-1)) and (27,e³,e²).

after.name: Question 18
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,{e}^{t-1}⟩$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t-1})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨{t}^{3}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,{e}^{t-1}⟩ & =c\,⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ {e}^{t}=c{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t-1}=c{e}^{t-1}\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we obtain that $c=1.$ Substituting $c=1$ into the first equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2}(t-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=0$, and $t=3.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{3},\,{e}^{0},\,{e}^{0-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,{e}^{-1}⟩ \\ r(3) & =⟨{3}^{3},\,{e}^{3},\,{e}^{3-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨27,\,{e}^{3},\,{e}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(0,1,{e}^{-1})$ and $(27,{e}^{3},{e}^{2}).$

Question 18

Given the curve r(t)=⟨t3,et,et−1⟩, find all points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
(1,0,e−1) and (27,e3,e2)
b
(27,e3,e2)
c
(0,1,0) and (27,e3,e2)
d
(0,1,e−1) and (27,e3,e2)
e
(0,1,e−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t):

r′(t)=⟨ddt(t3),ddt(et),ddt(et−1)⟩=⟨3t2,et,et−1⟩

The vectors r′(t) and r(t) are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r(t0)=cr′(t0). So, we have

r(t)=cr′(t)⟨t3,et,et−1⟩=c⟨3t2,et,et−1⟩.

Equating the components gives:

{t3=c(3t2)et=cetet−1=cet−1

From the second and third equations, we obtain that c=1. Substituting c=1 into the first equation gives:

t3=3t2t3−3t2=0t2(t−3)=0

Therefore, r and r′ are parallel only at the points corresponding to t=0, and t=3.

Finally, since r(0)=⟨03,e0,e0−1⟩=⟨0,1,e−1⟩r(3)=⟨33,e3,e3−1⟩=⟨27,e3,e2⟩,

we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are parallel at the points (0,1,e−1) and (27,e3,e2).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,{e}^{t-1}⟩$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t-1})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨{t}^{3}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,{e}^{t-1}⟩ & =c\,⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ {e}^{t}=c{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t-1}=c{e}^{t-1}\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we obtain that $c=1.$ Substituting $c=1$ into the first equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2}(t-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=0$, and $t=3.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{3},\,{e}^{0},\,{e}^{0-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,{e}^{-1}⟩ \\ r(3) & =⟨{3}^{3},\,{e}^{3},\,{e}^{3-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨27,\,{e}^{3},\,{e}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(0,1,{e}^{-1})$ and $(27,{e}^{3},{e}^{2}).$

Question 19
?

Given the curve r(t)=e2ti+(t2+t+12)j, find all points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
(e,54) and (e−2,12)
b
(e,54)
c
(e2,52)
d
(1,12)
e
(1,12) and (e2,52)
Submit

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨2e^(2t),2t+1⟩. Since e^(2t)>0, parallelism requires r'(t)=2r(t). Hence 2t+1=2(t²+t+1/2), giving 2t²=0 and only t=0. The point is r(0)=(1,1/2).

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)={e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2}=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$

Given the curve r(t)=e2ti+(t2+t+12)j, find all points at which r′(t) and r(t) are parallel.

a
(e,54) and (e−2,12)
b
(e,54)
c
(e2,52)
d
(1,12)
e
(1,12) and (e2,52)

EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t):

r′(t)=ddt(e2t)i+ddt(t2+t+12)j=2e2ti+(2t+1)j.

The vectors r′(t) and r(t) are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r(t0)=cr′(t0). So, we have

r(t)=cr′(t)e2ti+(t2+t+12)j=c(2e2ti+(2t+1)j)e2ti+(t2+t+12)j=2ce2ti+c(2t+1)j.

Equating the coefficients of i and j gives:

{e2t=2ce2tt2+t+12=c(2t+1)

From the first equation, we obtain c=12. Substituting c=12 into the second equality, we get t2+t+12=12(2t+1)t2=0t=0.

Therefore, r and r′ are parallel at the point corresponding to t=0.

Finally, since r(0)=e0i+(02+0+12)j=i+12j, we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are parallel at the point (1,12).

verification.explanation: Since r'(t)=⟨2e^(2t),2t+1⟩ and e^(2t)>0, parallelism requires r(t)=(1/2)r'(t). The second component gives t²+t+1/2=t+1/2, hence only t=0. Thus r(0)=(1,1/2), confirming option d and the revealed solution.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)={e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2}=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$

decision.explanation: r'(t)=⟨1,3t²,2t⟩. Writing r(t)=c r'(t), the first component gives c=t. The second gives 2+t³=3t³, hence t=1; this also satisfies 1+t²=2t². Therefore the only point is r(1)=(1,3,2).

after.name: Question 20
after.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$   

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+{t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k & =c(i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}t=c \\ 2+{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ 1+{t}^{2}=c(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $t=c.$ Substituting $c=t$ into the second equality gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}2+{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{3} \\ 2 & =2{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{3} & =1 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the equation $1+{t}^{2}=c(2t).$
Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =i+(2+{1}^{3})\,j+(1+{1}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+3\,j+2\,k,\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the derivative of r(t):

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(2+t3)j+ddt(1+t2)k=i+3t2j+2tk

The vectors r′(t) and r(t) are parallel for some specific value t0 of the parameter t if and only if there exists a constant c such that r(t0)=cr′(t0). So, we have

r(t)=cr′(t)ti+(2+t3)j+(1+t2)k=c(i+3t2j+2tk).

Equating the coefficients of i,j, and k gives:

{t=c2+t3=c(3t2)1+t2=c(2t)

From the first equation we obtain t=c. Substituting c=t into the second equality gives

2+t3=3t32=2t3t3=1t=1

This satisfies also the equation 1+t2=c(2t). Therefore, r and r′ are parallel only at the point corresponding to t=1.

Finally, since r(1)=i+(2+13)j+(1+12)k=i+3j+2k, we conclude that r(t) and r′(t) are parallel at the point P(1,3,2).

content.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
content.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$   

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+{t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k & =c(i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}t=c \\ 2+{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ 1+{t}^{2}=c(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $t=c.$ Substituting $c=t$ into the second equality gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}2+{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{3} \\ 2 & =2{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{3} & =1 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the equation $1+{t}^{2}=c(2t).$
Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =i+(2+{1}^{3})\,j+(1+{1}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+3\,j+2\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $P(1,3,2).$
